newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian metals-trade hopeful of import duty relief.
newsitem.headline: Indian metals-trade hopeful of import duty relief.

text.p: India's non-ferrous industry and trade are hopeful of a reduction in import duty on all major non-ferrous raw materials in the country's national budget for 1997/98 (April/March), trade leaders said on Wednesday.
The budget will be presented to parliament on Friday.
"We are expecting an import duty relief of at least 5.0 percent on all non-ferrous metals in the budget," said Sharad Parikh, president of the Bombay Metals Exchange.
India imports most major non-ferrous metals. These include copper wirebars and wire rods and cathodes, zinc and tin slabs, lead ingots and nickel cathods.
Parikh said the trade is also expecting the government to maintain a differential in import duty on raw materials and semi-finished products.
"We are hopeful the government will raise import duty on semi-finished products to help protect domestic units supplying raw materials," he said.
At present, import duty on raw material and semi-finished items is the same at 51.80 percent, including excise and taxes.
"Users prefer imported semi-finished products to local raw materials," Parikh said.
"We have asked for a differential of 15 percent and we are hopeful that it will at least be 10 percent," he said.
Parikh said the exchange had also pleaded for a reduction in excise duty in the budget.
On Tuesday, in an address to members of the exchange, Parikh said metal importers in Bombay faced a stiff 2.5 percent octroi or entry tax which made their products economically unviable.
"It must be brought down to 1.0 percent," Parikh said.
He said heavy fluctuations in the prices of non-ferrous metals abroad had badly affected the economy of Indian metals industry and trade in the last one year.
"We expect the budget to help the industry and trade to recover," Parikh said.

In the week to Wednesday, copper suffered a loss of 100 rupees to 12,800 rupees per quintal (100 kgs) while zinc gained 200 rupees to 7,300 rupees per quintal. Nickel was active and gained 300 rupees to 37,400 rupees per quintal. Aluminium, lead and tin were steady in dull trade.
